a: This is a copy of the letter Jeremiah sent
t: A letter, a copy and a title
p: The Greek calls it a 'copy' of Jeremiah's letter. Greek Bibles print it as its own book.
b: The heading uses antigraphon, 'copy', the word for a duplicate of an official letter. In Codex Vaticanus and Codex Alexandrinus the work is titled Epistolē Ieremiou, 'Letter of Jeremiah', and Alexandrinus ends with a line naming 'Jeremiah the prophet, Baruch, Lamentations and Letter' together (Swete's notes). Greek and Orthodox Bibles keep it as a separate book after Lamentations; the Latin Vulgate made it the last chapter of Baruch, and Catholic Bibles and the KJV Apocrypha follow that. This site numbers the verses as Swete and the Göttingen edition do (72 verses). The Vulgate also has 72 verses, but its divisions differ in places: its 6:53 holds the crows of this site's 6:54. The KJV counts the heading as verse 1, so its numbers run one higher (73 verses).

a: what he had been ordered to say by God
t: Is this the letter of Jeremiah 29?
p: The Bible's Jeremiah sent the exiles a letter, but it is a different one, and no Hebrew copy of this one exists.
b: Jeremiah 29 gives the text of a real letter Jeremiah sent from Jerusalem to the exiles: "Build houses and settle in them" (Jeremiah 29:5) and "Seek the peace of the city I sent you to as exiles" (Jeremiah 29:7). That letter says nothing about idols. This one says nothing about houses, gardens or the peace of Babylon. It is a sermon against idols, built from Jeremiah 10 and Isaiah 44, written as a letter. Catholic and Orthodox churches read it as Scripture under Jeremiah's name; Protestants and Jews do not count it. Sean Adams reads it as one of the writings of the period composed in Jeremiah's name. The book's opening pages weigh this (see Jeremiah's card, "Are Baruch and the Letter of Jeremiah part of the Bible?").

a: because of those sins
p: The letter starts where the prophets do: Babylon comes because Judah sinned.
b: The captivity is God's judgment, not Babylon's victory over Judah's God. This is the reading of the exile in Jeremiah (25:8–11 in his book) and in the covenant warnings of Deuteronomy 28:36, and it is the theme of the confession in Baruch 1:15–3:8. It matters for what follows. If the LORD sent his people to Babylon, Babylon's gods did not beat him, and the captives have no reason to fear them.

a: as long as seven generations
p: Jeremiah gave seventy years. The letter gives seven generations, a longer time, and scholars use it to date the letter.
b: Jeremiah says the nations "will serve the king of Babylon seventy years" (Jeremiah 25:11; compare Jeremiah 29:10). The letter says "seven generations", which is longer. Scholars use the number for dating. Taking a generation as forty years (he points to Judges 3:11), Daniel Harrington counts 280 years from 597 BC and reaches 317 BC. David deSilva reports scholars who take 317–306 BC, 280 years after the first or second deportation, as the latest date for a Hebrew original of the letter, since a writer would hardly change Jeremiah's term into one that had already run out; he adds that a 'generation' is too loose a measure for precise dates. J. Alberto Soggin compares the problem to Daniel's, since Daniel 9 also rereads the seventy years. Read as Jeremiah's own words, as the heading presents them, the number promises a longer stay than his seventy years. Either way the letter here goes beyond Jeremiah's words.

a: Then I will lead you out of there in peace
p: The letter slips from Jeremiah's voice into God's: 'I will lead you out', and 'my angel' in 6:6.
b: The heading says Jeremiah wrote what God ordered him to say (6:1), and here the speaker is God himself: "I will lead you out" (exaxō, the verb of the exodus from Egypt in the Greek of Exodus). In 6:6 the same voice says "my angel is with you". The rest of the letter is argument in the writer's own voice, and in 6:68 he even says "to us". The prophets move between their own words and God's in the same way.
orig: ἐξάξω ὑμᾶς (exaxō hymas), 'I will lead you out'

a: these gods
p: The letter calls the statues theoi, 'gods', all the way through, so the Plain does too, and keeps 'idols' for 6:72.
b: The Greek calls the statues theoi, 'gods', from the first sight of them (6:3) to the end, and the whole argument is the refrain that they "are not gods" (6:14). So this site renders theoi 'gods' in every verse of the letter, the worshipers' own word turned against them. With 'idols' the refrain would say they are not idols, and the questions of 6:39, 6:44, 6:56 and 6:63, whether they can be called gods at all, would lose their point. The ordinary word for an idol, eidōlon, comes only once, in the last verse, and only there does the Plain say 'idols' (6:72). The Greek refers to the gods sometimes with a neuter 'them' (auta, 6:5, 6:22, 6:38), agreeing with neuter words for 'wooden' and 'gold-plated' things (6:7, 6:38), and sometimes with a masculine 'them' (autous, 6:14, 6:28), as for persons; English 'them' cannot show the difference. At 6:3 the Latin Vulgate (and the Douay-Rheims) adds 'stone' to the list.

a: carried high on shoulders
p: The letter pictures statues carried through bowing crowds, a sight Isaiah also mocks.
b: The letter pictures the gods "carried high on shoulders" through crowds that bow before and behind them (6:5), and comes back to it at 6:25. Isaiah mocks the same sight: "The images you carried in procession are packed up as freight" (Isaiah 46:1), and the worshipers "hoist it on their shoulders and haul it" (Isaiah 46:7). When and where the letter was written is debated (see the chapter page), so the scene may come from the writer's own city or from the prophets and from what was told of Babylon. The letter presents it as the test its readers will face.

a: grow like the foreigners
p: The Greek says 'having become like... you become like'. Some see a Hebrew idiom under it.
b: The Greek repeats the verb: aphomoiōthentes ... aphomoiōthēte, 'having become like the foreigners you become like them'. Carey Moore took this as a Hebrew way of stressing a verb (the 'infinitive absolute'), one of his reasons for thinking the letter was first written in Hebrew. Benjamin Wright, in the introduction to the NETS translation, doubts it: the Greek is a play on sound, and the two verbs are not side by side as the Hebrew idiom would have them. Allophyloi, 'foreigners', is literally 'people of another tribe'.
orig: ἀφομοιωθέντες τοῖς ἀλλοφύλοις ἀφομοιωθῆτε (aphomoiōthentes tois allophylois aphomoiōthēte)

a: bowing down to them
p: The same verb, proskyneō, is the crowd's bowing and the captives' inner worship.
b: Proskyneō is the bodily act of bowing low, and the word for worship. The letter uses it twice in one verse: the crowds bow down to the gods, and the captives say in their minds that the Lord is the one who must be worshiped. The point is that the outward scene does not decide who is worshiped. Compare the three young men who would not bow to Nebuchadnezzar's gold image (Daniel 3:18).

a: Master
p: Despota, the word for a master of slaves, is a title of God in Greek prayers.
b: The captives address God as Despota, 'Master', the owner of a household and its slaves. The Greek of Jeremiah uses the same word in the prophet's own prayers, for Hebrew Adonai (Jeremiah 1:6; Jeremiah 4:10 in Greek, 'Master, Lord'). The prayer is a confession of ownership: the captives belong to their Master, not to Babylon's gods. This site renders the title 'Master' in every Greek book (as in Judith, 2 Maccabees and Wisdom).

a: in your own mind
p: Around AD 211 Tertullian quoted this verse to Christians tempted to go along with idol worship.
b: In his Scorpiace (chapter 8), written for Christians under threat of death, Tertullian quotes these words as Jeremiah's (in S. Thelwall's translation): "say in your mind, Our duty is to worship You, O Lord." He sets them beside the three young men who would not worship the king's gold image, and uses them to say that a believer must not join the crowd even to save his life. Dianoia is the mind, the place of thought and intention; the Vulgate and the KJV say 'hearts'.

a: my angel is with you
t: The angel who goes with God's people
p: The words echo God's angel who went ahead of Israel out of Egypt.
b: At Sinai God said, "I am sending an angel in front of you to keep you safe on the way" (Exodus 23:20), and after the golden calf, "my angel will go ahead of you" (Exodus 32:34). The letter gives the captives the same guard on the way into exile. Whether every believer has such an angel is a question the churches answer differently; the card is at Tobit 5, Psalm 91 and Matthew 18:10, and is not repeated here.
r: Exodus 23:20; Exodus 32:34; Psalm 34:7; Psalm 91:11; Matthew 18:10; Tobit 5:22

a: they cannot speak
p: The letter starts from Jeremiah 10 and Psalm 115, which mock idols with tongues and no voice.
b: Jeremiah says, "Like a scarecrow in a cucumber field, they cannot speak" (Jeremiah 10:5), and "the image he casts is a lie" (Jeremiah 10:14). The psalm says, "A mouth they have, but they cannot speak" (Psalm 115:5). Habakkuk has "worthless gods that cannot speak" (Habakkuk 2:18). The letter adds a sharp detail: the tongue itself was planed smooth by a woodworker. The Greek pseudē, 'false things', is rendered 'a lie' here and at 6:44 and 6:50.

a: a girl who loves pretty things
p: The gods get crowns the way a young woman gets jewelry. Jeremiah used the same picture against Israel.
b: Parthenos philokosmos is a young woman who loves ornaments. Jeremiah asked, "Does a young woman forget her ornaments" (Jeremiah 2:32), and said Israel had forgotten God. The letter turns the picture on the idols: they are dolls, decked out by others. The Vulgate reads the verse a little differently, but the sense is the same.

a: the priests slip gold and silver away from their gods
p: The priests know the gods will not notice. Bel and the Dragon tells a similar story.
b: The letter's priests behave as if they knew their gods were nothing: they steal from them (6:9), sell the sacrifices (6:27), take the gods' clothes for their families (6:32) and run when fire comes (6:54). The story of Bel and the Dragon, one of the Additions to Daniel, makes the same charge: Daniel shows the king that Bel's priests come in through secret doors and eat the food set before the god. Both are satire. They do not describe how the priests of Babylon saw their own work.

a: the prostitutes up on the roof
p: The Greek says 'on the roof'. Two great codices spell the word slightly differently.
b: Codex Vaticanus has stegos, 'roof': the women may be on a flat roof, perhaps of the temple itself. Codex Alexandrinus and Codex Marchalianus (Q) spell it tegos, another form of the word (Swete's notes). The Latin Vulgate tells it differently: the priests give the gold to prostitutes and then take it back from them to adorn their gods. The letter returns to sex and the cult at 6:42–43.
orig: ταῖς ἐπὶ τοῦ στέγους πόρναις (tais epi tou stegous pornais)

a: And they dress them in clothes as if they were people
p: The 'them' who are dressed are the gods, as the end of the verse shows.
b: The KJV can be read as if the priests dress the prostitutes, but the Greek names the ones dressed at the end of the verse: "silver gods, gold gods and wooden ones." Jeremiah describes the same care: "Violet and purple cloth is their clothing" (Jeremiah 10:9). The letter keeps coming back to the clothes: purple robes that cannot save them from decay (6:11), robes taken by the priests (6:32) and by thieves (6:57), and purple that rots (6:71).

a: from tarnish and from being eaten away
p: The Greek says 'from rust and foods'. The KJV and Vulgate have 'rust and moth'.
b: Ios is the corrosion on metal, 'rust' or 'tarnish' (again at 6:23). Brōmata normally means 'foods', which is odd here. Carey Moore thought a Hebrew word that can mean 'food' or 'a devourer' (an insect such as the moth) was read the wrong way, a sign of a Hebrew original; the NETS introduction reports his argument. The Plain gives 'being eaten away', which fits both the Greek and the sense. The Vulgate and the KJV say 'moth', and Jesus pairs the same two enemies: "Here moths and rust eat them away" (Matthew 6:19).
orig: ἀπὸ ἰοῦ καὶ βρωμάτων (apo iou kai brōmatōn)

a: The dust of the house
p: The letter calls a temple a 'house', as the Bible calls the temple 'the LORD's house'.
b: The Greek says oikia and oikos, 'house', for the god's temple (6:12, 6:16, 6:17, 6:19, 6:20, 6:30, 6:54), as Hebrew bayit is used for 'the LORD's house'. The Plain keeps 'house', so the reader sees the joke: the god's home fills with dust, smoke, bats and cats, while the true God's house was filled with his glory (1 Kings 8:11). At 6:58 the same word is an ordinary home.

a: one of them holds a scepter
p: The statues carry signs of a king and a warrior, which they cannot use.
b: The letter describes a god holding a scepter, the rod of a ruler and judge, and another with a dagger and an ax in his hand (6:14). The mockery is in the gap between the emblem and the power: the judge cannot punish, and the warrior cannot defend himself. Jeremiah's verdict on idols is that "They can do no harm, and they can do no good either" (Jeremiah 10:5); the letter makes that line into a list.

a: This makes it plain that they are not gods.
p: In some ten places the letter sums up: they are not gods, so do not fear them.
b: The refrain comes in two forms. The command form, 'they are not gods ... have no fear of them', ends 6:14, 6:22, 6:28, 6:64 and 6:68. The question form, 'how can they be thought of as gods, or called gods?', ends 6:39 and 6:44 and opens 6:56; it has no 'do not fear'. Related lines stand at 6:29, 6:49, 6:51, 6:63 and 6:71. The Plain keeps the same English wherever the Greek is the same. At 6:22 the Greek verb is a present (phobeisthe) where the other command refrains have an aorist (phobēthēte); the difference need not mean 'keep on fearing', so the Plain says simply 'So do not fear them' there (see the variant). At 6:68 the line begins 'therefore' (dio). The words come from Jeremiah: "Do not be afraid of them" (Jeremiah 10:5), mē phobēthēte auta in the Greek of Jeremiah. Moore read gnōrimoi, 'known', here as a misread Hebrew word; Wright, introducing the NETS translation, answers that the Greek word can just as well be an adjective.
orig: ὅθεν γνώριμοί εἰσιν οὐκ ὄντες θεοί· μὴ οὖν φοβηθῆτε αὐτούς

a: Dust from the feet of everyone coming in fills their eyes
p: Psalm 115 says idols have eyes but cannot see. Here they cannot even blink away dust.
b: The psalm says, "eyes they have, but they cannot see" (Psalm 115:5), and Deuteronomy speaks of gods "which cannot see or hear or eat or smell" (Deuteronomy 4:28). The letter makes it concrete: worshipers walk in, kick up dust, and it settles in the open eyes of a god that cannot close them. The lamps of 6:18 make the same point.

a: as for a man who has wronged a king
p: The god is locked in like a prisoner awaiting execution, not guarded like a king.
b: The Greek is crowded, and translations divide its clauses differently. The sense is clear enough: the courtyards are fenced in as they would be around a man who has offended a king or a man led off to die. The priests' locks and bars are meant to protect the gods, but they make the god's house look like a jail, and they show that the god cannot protect himself from robbers.
orig: ὥσπερ τινὶ ἠδικηκότι βασιλέα (hōsper tini ēdikēkoti basilea)

a: Their hearts
p: The 'hearts' of these gods can only be the inside of a wooden statue, which insects eat out.
b: Kardia is 'heart'. Here the hearts of the gods can only be the inside of the wooden statues, which creeping things lick out while the gods feel nothing. The joke cuts two ways: a god with a heart should feel and care, and these have hearts of rotting wood. The Vulgate reads 'serpents' for the creeping things.
orig: τὰς δὲ καρδίας αὐτῶν (tas de kardias autōn)

a: The smoke from the house has turned their faces black
t: Claude's theory: a house filled with the wrong things
p: My suggestion: verses 12 to 21 read like the reverse of the temple filled with God's glory.
b: My own reading, offered as a theory. When Solomon dedicated the temple, "The LORD's glory filled the LORD's house" (1 Kings 8:11), and in Isaiah's vision before God's throne "smoke kept filling the house" (Isaiah 6:4). In 6:12–21 the gods' house is also full: of dust from feet, smoke from lamps, creeping things, bats, swallows, birds and cats. Its smoke only blackens the god's face. The letter does not cite 1 Kings 8 or Isaiah 6, so this is a pattern the reader may see, not something the writer says. I have not found this pairing argued in a source.

a: and the cats as well
p: Cats appear nowhere in the 66 books. Egypt honored them; here they sit on a god.
b: Ailouroi, 'cats', are named nowhere in the 66 books, and nowhere else in the books outside them that this site has in English (Tobit, Judith, Wisdom of Solomon, Sirach, Baruch 1–5, 1 Esdras, 1 Maccabees, 2 Maccabees, 3 Maccabees and 1 Enoch). Egyptians treated cats as sacred: Herodotus says that when a house cat died a natural death the household shaved their eyebrows, and that dead cats were embalmed and buried at Bubastis (Histories 2.66–67, Macaulay's translation). In the letter the cat is only another creature that climbs over a helpless god.

a: not one has breath in it
p: The prophets' sharpest line against idols: there is no breath, no spirit, in them.
b: Pneuma is breath and spirit. Jeremiah says of the cast image that "there is no breath in them" (Jeremiah 10:14), and Habakkuk of the plated idol that "there is no breath inside it at all" (Habakkuk 2:19). In Genesis 2:7 life begins when God breathes into the man. The gods bought "at great cost" lack the one thing money cannot buy.
orig: ἐν οἷς οὐκ ἔστιν πνεῦμα (en hois ouk estin pneuma)

a: With no feet, they have to be carried on shoulders
p: Isaiah's great contrast: Babylon carries its gods, but the LORD carries his people.
b: Jeremiah says, "Someone always has to pick them up, for they take no steps" (Jeremiah 10:5), and Isaiah that the worshipers "hoist it on their shoulders and haul it" (Isaiah 46:7). Isaiah sets that beside God's promise to Israel, that he has carried them from birth and will carry them to old age (Isaiah 46:3–4). The letter keeps the first half of the contrast; its readers knew the second.

a: Offerings are laid out for them the way they are laid out for the dead
p: Food set before a statue is as useless as food set beside a corpse.
b: The letter sets the gifts laid before the gods beside the gifts laid out for the dead: a god that cannot get up when it falls is no different from a body. Bel and the Dragon, one of the Additions to Daniel, pictures the large daily supply of flour, sheep and oil spent on Bel's statue in Babylon. Israel's law forbade giving any of the holy tithe to the dead: "I have not given any of it for the dead" (Deuteronomy 26:14). Psalm 106:28 speaks of eating "sacrifices of the dead".

a: pass none of it on to anyone poor or weak
p: Israel's law sent part of the holy food to the poor. The letter says Babylon's priests keep it all.
b: In Deuteronomy the tithe feeds "the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow" (Deuteronomy 14:29), and the feasts are shared with the poor (Deuteronomy 16:11). The letter judges Babylon by Israel's law: what is offered to the gods is sold for profit or salted down at home, and none goes to those in need. The same measure returns at 6:37, where the gods have no mercy for the widow or the orphan.

a: A woman in her monthly bleeding and a woman fresh from childbirth touch their sacrifices
p: In Israel such a woman could not touch holy things. The writer judges Babylon by Israel's law.
b: Leviticus says a woman after childbirth "must not touch anything holy or come into the sanctuary" until her days of purifying are over (Leviticus 12:4), and treats the monthly flow the same way (Leviticus 15:19). This is not a moral charge against the women. It is a mark of what the writer counts holy: a sacrifice that anyone may handle, in any state, cannot belong to a real god. The verse shows the writer's own standard: he judges Babylon's worship by the purity laws of Leviticus.

a: women lay out food
t: Women at the table of the gods
p: The verb means to set something before someone, as a meal.
b: Paratithēmi is to set food before a guest. The question and its answer are ironic: is this what makes them gods? The complaint itself is not spelled out. It may be that women, not priests, serve the gods; or simply that a god who must be fed by anyone at all is no god. Jeremiah saw women in Judah bake cakes for the Queen of Heaven (Jeremiah 7:18; Jeremiah 44:19).

a: the priests sit on their seats
p: The Greek verb is rare. The ancient copies and translations all take it as 'sit'.
b: Codex Vaticanus has diphreuousin, a rare verb. Codex Marchalianus (Q) has the common kathizousin, 'they sit', and Codex Alexandrinus diaphtheirousin, 'they destroy', which makes no sense here (Swete's notes). The Vulgate (sedent) and the KJV both say 'sit'. The Plain follows that sense.

a: ripped tunics, shaved heads, shaved beards
p: Israel's priests were forbidden to shave their heads and beards or tear their clothes.
b: Torn clothes and shaved heads and beards were signs of mourning (Jeremiah 41:5). Israel's law forbade them to priests: "Priests must not make their heads bald, or shave the corners of their beards" (Leviticus 21:5), and the high priest must not "tear his clothes" (Leviticus 21:10). The letter's priests sit in their gods' house as mourners, wailing as at a funeral meal (6:31). Ezekiel saw women in the temple "weeping for Tammuz" (Ezekiel 8:14). The letter does not say whom Babylon's priests mourn.

a: the meal held after a death
p: Perideipnon is the meal for mourners after a funeral.
b: Perideipnon is the meal held for mourners after a burial. Jeremiah mentions the bread and cup of comfort given to mourners (Jeremiah 16:7). The letter's picture is pointed: the priests behave as if their god were dead. The mourners at this meal are the god's own priests, sitting in his house.

a: They cannot set up a king or remove one
p: In Daniel, God 'removes kings and sets kings up'. Babylon's gods cannot.
b: Daniel's prayer says of God, "he removes kings and he sets kings up" (Daniel 2:21), and Nebuchadnezzar learns that "the Most High is ruler over the kingdom of humankind" (Daniel 4:17). The letter denies them that power here and at 6:52 and 6:65.

a: they will never come after him for it
p: Israel's God holds people to their vows. These gods cannot even do that.
b: The law says, "When you make a vow to the LORD your God, do not be slow to pay it, for the LORD your God will surely ask it of you" (Deuteronomy 23:21; compare Ecclesiastes 5:4). In the Greek of Deuteronomy the verb is ekzēteō, 'require'; the letter uses its close relative epizēteō. A god who cannot call in a debt has no claim on anyone. Here the letter agrees with the 66 books exactly.

a: A widow gets no mercy from them, and an orphan gets no kindness.
p: 6:35 to 6:37 list, one by one, what the Psalms say the LORD does.
b: Psalm 146 praises the God who "wins justice for those crushed by wrong" (Psalm 146:7), and "The LORD gives sight to the blind" (Psalm 146:8); he "keeps watch over foreigners" and lifts up the orphan and the widow (Psalm 146:9). Psalm 68:5 calls God "a father to orphans". The letter's list in 6:35–37 (rescue from death, the weak saved from the strong, sight for the blind, help in trouble, mercy for the widow and the orphan) is that portrait turned to its opposite.

a: they bring Bel
p: Bel means 'lord'. Jeremiah pairs Bel with Marduk, the chief god of Babylon.
b: Bēl means 'lord'. The prophets name him among Babylon's gods: "Bel has bowed down; Nebo is doubled over" (Isaiah 46:1), and "Bel is put to shame; / Marduk is shattered" (Jeremiah 50:2, poetry). Since Jeremiah sets the two names side by side, Bel here is most likely Marduk, Babylon's chief god, under his title. Bel and the Dragon, one of the Additions to Daniel, tells how Daniel proved that Bel's statue ate nothing. The Chaldeans are the Babylonians, named after the people whose kings ruled the city in Nebuchadnezzar's day.
r: Isaiah 46:1; Jeremiah 50:2; Jeremiah 51:44; Additions to Daniel

a: beg for him to speak
p: The Greek does not say whether the mute man or Bel is to speak, and the Plain leaves it open.
b: The Greek says the Chaldeans bring Bel and "ask to give voice" (phōnēsai), without saying who is to give it. Benjamin Wright, introducing the NETS translation, calls 6:40–41 perhaps the best example in the letter of Greek that makes little sense, and says this clause does not make clear whether the Chaldeans expect the mute man to speak or Bel. The Latin Vulgate has them bring the mute man to Bel, "asking him to speak" (postulantes ab eo loqui), and the KJV has them "intreat Bel that he may speak"; both leave 'he' as open as the Greek. Codex Alexandrinus reads 'then to speak' (tote lalēsai) in place of 'to give voice' (Swete's notes). The Plain's 'him' is left open on purpose: it can be the man or Bel.

a: they cannot leave those gods behind
t: Do they leave their gods or not?
p: The Greek says they cannot leave their gods. The Vulgate says they will leave them.
b: The Greek reads, 'they themselves, having understood, cannot leave them, for they have no sense'. That is, the Chaldeans see their god fail and still cannot give him up. The Vulgate says the opposite, that when they understand they will leave them, "for their gods have no sense". Wright notes that the NRSV and Moore also make the Chaldeans abandon their gods, against the Greek grammar. The Plain follows the Greek, and leaves open whether "they have no sense" means the Chaldeans or the gods.
orig: οὐ δύνανται αὐτοὶ νοήσαντες καταλιπεῖν αὐτά (ou dynantai autoi noēsantes katalipein auta)

a: the women, wearing cords
p: Herodotus tells of Babylonian women with cords on their heads who sat at a temple for strangers.
b: Herodotus says that every Babylonian woman once in her life sat in the precinct of Aphrodite "with a wreath of cord about their heads" until a stranger threw a silver coin into her lap and lay with her (Histories 1.199, Macaulay's translation). Stephanie Budin has argued that sacred prostitution of this kind did not exist in the ancient world, and that the Letter of Jeremiah, consciously or not, took the custom from Herodotus. Vinciane Pirenne-Delforge, reviewing the book, agreed with its main conclusion and found the arguments of this chapter good, but did not think Budin's reading of Herodotus himself ended the debate. So the verse may describe a real custom, or a Greek story about Babylon that the writer knew. The Vulgate has the women burn olive stones, not bran.

a: her cord was never broken
p: The woman who was taken mocks her neighbor, whose cord is still whole.
b: The woman who has been taken boasts over her neighbor: that one was not thought as worthy, and her cord was never broken. The letter does not explain the cord further, and Herodotus, who describes the cords (see 6:42), says nothing about breaking them. Israel's law forbade a father to make his daughter a prostitute (Leviticus 19:29).

a: Everything done for them is a lie.
p: A tiny Greek papyrus from Qumran Cave 7 is thought to hold 6:43–44, though it is too small to be sure.
b: A small Greek papyrus fragment from Qumran Cave 7, 7Q2, is thought to hold 6:43–44, in a form of the text later found in the Lucianic Greek manuscripts and the Syriac. It has only twenty-two letters, so, as Sean Adams notes, the identification is not certain. It was published in the third volume of Discoveries in the Judaean Desert, and Daniel Harrington dates the manuscript about 100 BC. If it is the Letter, it is the oldest copy, and the letter existed in Greek by then and was kept at Qumran.

a: Woodworkers and goldsmiths built them
p: Hosea says of the calf, 'A craftsman made it, and it is no god.' The letter argues the same way.
b: The argument is simple: what a craftsman makes cannot be greater than the craftsman. Hosea says of Samaria's calf, "A craftsman made it, and it is no god" (Hosea 8:6). Isaiah adds that "The craftsmen are mere humans" (Isaiah 44:11). The letter goes one step further in 6:46–47: the makers die, so how can their work outlast them?
r: Hosea 8:6; Isaiah 44:11–13; Jeremiah 10:9; Wisdom of Solomon 15:16–17

a: where to hide along with them
p: The prophets picture gods carried off in war. Here the priests hide with them.
b: Isaiah sees Bel and Nebo loaded on animals, and "they themselves have gone into captivity" (Isaiah 46:2). Jeremiah says "Chemosh will go out into exile, / his priests and his officials together" (Jeremiah 48:7, poetry). The letter's priests, facing war, plan where to hide with their gods, so the gods need saving like any other valuables.

a: something human hands have made
p: The Greek phrase is word for word the Greek of Psalm 115:4.
b: The Greek erga cheirōn anthrōpōn, 'works of human hands', is exactly the Greek of Psalm 115:4 (Psalm 113:12 in the Greek numbering), so the Plain uses this site's wording of that psalm: "something human hands have made" (Psalm 115:4). The Wisdom of Solomon uses the same phrase of those who called such things gods (Wisdom of Solomon 13:10), and at Ephesus Paul was accused of saying "gods produced by hands are not gods" (Acts 19:26).
r: Psalm 115:4; Psalm 135:15; Wisdom of Solomon 13:10; Acts 19:26; Acts 17:29

a: no work of God is in them
p: The letter says idols are nothing. Paul says that, and also that demons stand behind them.
b: For the letter the gods are only things: wood, metal and cloth, with "no work of God" in them. Paul agrees that "an idol is nothing in the world" (1 Corinthians 8:4), but adds that "what they sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God" (1 Corinthians 10:20), echoing Deuteronomy 32:17; Revelation 9:20 lists "demons and idols" together. The letter never mentions demons. It does not conflict with the 66 books, but it gives only half of their picture.

a: nor send rain down on people
p: Jeremiah asks whether any idol can make it rain. The letter says these gods cannot.
b: Jeremiah asks, "Can any of the nations' empty idols make it rain?" (Jeremiah 14:22), and answers that the LORD does. Elijah's contest on Carmel ended in rain from Israel's God (1 Kings 18:41–45), and Paul told the people of Lystra that God showed his goodness by giving rain from heaven (Acts 14:17).

a: They are like crows between the sky and the earth
p: An odd simile. Moore thought a Hebrew 'like clouds' was misread as 'like crows'.
b: The Greek korōnai are crows (the Vulgate has 'little crows'). The picture is hard to place: perhaps birds that flap about and achieve nothing. The NETS introduction reports that the Syriac has 'ravens', and that Moore suggested the Greek translator misread a Hebrew word for 'like clouds' as 'like crows', which would fit the sky and earth better. That theory assumes a Hebrew original, which is not certain (see 6:4).

a: better a wooden post in a palace than the false gods
p: Three times: a king, a pot, a door, even a post is more useful 'than the false gods'.
b: The Greek repeats ē hoi pseudeis theoi, 'than the false gods', three times, and the Plain keeps the repetition. The list sinks as it goes: a brave king, a useful pot, a door that guards a house, a wooden post that holds up a roof. Each does what it was made to do. The gods, made of the same wood, do nothing.
orig: ἢ οἱ ψευδεῖς θεοί (ē hoi pseudeis theoi)

a: they do as they are told
p: Sun, moon, stars, lightning, wind, clouds and fire all obey God. The idols do nothing.
b: Babylon honored the sun, moon and stars as gods. The letter treats them as servants sent on tasks (compare Baruch 3:34–35, where the stars answer when God calls them). Deuteronomy warns Israel not to bow to "the sun, the moon and the stars" (Deuteronomy 4:19); Psalm 148 calls them to praise God, with "the storm wind that carries out his word" (Psalm 148:8). Paul argues from the same created order that God's power is "visible to the mind in what he has made" (Romans 1:20). Here the letter agrees with the 66 books.

a: once God orders them
t: The only God in the argument
p: God is named only three times in the letter: in the heading, at 6:50 and here.
b: After the heading (6:1), God is named only at 6:50 ("no work of God is in them") and here, where he orders the clouds. The letter spends nearly all its words on the idols and almost none describing God. That is part of its method: once the gods are shown to be nothing, the reader is left with the Master of 6:5, who rules the sky.

a: They will never put signs in the sky for the nations to see
p: Babylon was famous for reading the sky. Jeremiah told Israel not to be frightened by it.
b: In Daniel the 'Chaldeans' are also Babylon's learned men, called in with the magicians and sorcerers to explain signs (Daniel 2:2). Jeremiah says, "Do not panic at the signs in the sky" (Jeremiah 10:2). The letter's claim is that the gods do not cause the signs: the sun and the moon shine because God sends them (6:59).

a: a scarecrow in a cucumber field that guards nothing
p: This line is in the Hebrew of Jeremiah 10:5 but not in its Greek. The writer knew the Hebrew.
b: Jeremiah says, "Like a scarecrow in a cucumber field, they cannot speak" (Jeremiah 10:5). The Greek of Jeremiah has no scarecrow there; it says the idols are 'hammered silver'. So the writer of the letter knew Jeremiah 10 in Hebrew, not only in Greek. Wright, introducing the NETS translation, makes this point. It is one of the stronger reasons for thinking the letter began in Hebrew or was written by someone at home in the Hebrew Bible.

a: a thornbush in a garden where every bird comes to sit
p: Rhamnos is the thornbush of Jotham's fable in the Greek of Judges 9.
b: Rhamnos is a thorny shrub. It is the word in the Greek of Judges 9:14 for the thornbush the trees ask to be their king ("Then all the trees said to the thornbush", Judges 9:14), a useless plant that offers shade it cannot give. Here every bird perches on it and nothing is kept off. The second picture, a body tossed into the dark, recalls the king who "will be buried the way a donkey is buried" (Jeremiah 22:19).
orig: τῇ ἐν κήπῳ ῥάμνῳ (tē en kēpō rhamnō)

a: keeps no idols
p: Here at last the word 'idols' appears, and the letter ends with no farewell.
b: Only here does the letter use eidōla, 'idols'. It ends without greetings, so it is a sermon in the form of a letter. Its message matches the 66 books: idols are made things, and those who trust God are better off without them (Psalm 115:8–11; 1 John 5:21, "guard yourselves against idols"). Where it goes beyond them is in its details of Babylonian worship, its seven generations (6:2) and its claim to be by Jeremiah. Codex Vaticanus and Codex Marchalianus end with the title 'Letter of Jeremiah' (Swete's notes).
